question: A 10-year-old patient has deteriorating daytime visual acuity and night vision. No choroidal perfusion was seen on any phases of her ﬂuorescein angiogram. What is the visual prognosis?

options.A: Vision will likely slowly decrease to worse than 20/400.
options.B: Vision is likely to suddenly decrease to about 20/40.
options.C: Vision will be normal in the daytime but worse than 20/400 at night only.
options.D: Vision will likely slowly decrease to about 20/100.

explanation: Stargardt disease is the most common hereditary macular dystrophy. It is bilateral, symmetric, and slowly progressive. Visual acuities level oﬀ at about between 20/50 and 20/200. Vision begins to slowly deteriorate between the ages of 8 and 15 years. Both photopic and scotopic vision is eventually aﬀected. daily pilocarpine drops.

question: A 4-year-old child who has unilateral, chronic uveitis is being treated with cycloplegics. What additional treatment can be done to best prevent amblyopia?
explanation: Cycloplegia is used in uveitis to prevent synechiae formation and decrease pain. However, cycloplegic drugs also blur vision, which can induce amblyopia. Indeed, amblyopia can be treated pharmacologically by using cycloplegics (atropine) on the fellow eye, rather than occlusion therapy, for this reason. Dispensing the full hyperopic prescription with a bifocal gives a clear image at near and distance, to decrease the risk of amblyopia. Orthoptics will not treat amblyopia in this situation. Patching is not the best treatment, as the aﬀected eye will be defocused for near work. Pilocarpine is contraindicated, because it will reverse the beneﬁcial eﬀects of the cycloplegics and may exacerbate inﬂammation. partial third nerve palsy A. 4% Explanation & Notes Discussion BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What is the most likely type of strabismus expected to be seen in a child with fetal alcohol syndrome?
explanation: Fetal alcohol syndrome is a craniofacial condition caused by in-utero exposure to ethanol due to heavy alcohol use by women during pregnancy. Fetal alcohol syndrome is characterized by prenatal and postnatal growth retardation, central nervous system abnormalities, and a wide spectrum of malformations, the most typical of these being craniofacial. Pertinent facial features include short palpebral ﬁssures, telecanthus, strabismus (especially esotropia), and ptosis. Ocular involvement can also include optic nerve hypoplasia (unilateral or bilateral) and increased tortuosity of the retinal vasculature. Nerve and muscle palsies and hypertropia are not components of fetal alcohol syndrome. inferotemporal.

question: What is the most common location of a teardrop-shaped iris coloboma?
explanation: Typical iris colobomas are in the inferonasal quadrant and are caused by the failure of the embryonic ﬁssure to close in the 5th week of gestation. These can be associated with chorioretinal and/or optic nerve colobomas. Atypical iris colobomas that occur in areas other than the inferonasal quadrant are not associated with more posterior colobomas. question: A 42-year-old man undergoes extraocular motility evaluation before strabismus surgery for poorly controlled intermittent exotropia. Visual acuity is 20/20 OU. What is the most appropriate test for measuring deviation in preparation for surgery?
explanation: Intermittent exotropia is a divergent form of strabismus that has a latent (controlled by fusion) component. Thus, to determine in a quantitative way the total amount of deviation, the prism alternate cover test is the most appropriate. The Krimsky and simultaneous prism and cover tests only determine the tropic component. The red glass test is not a satisfactory test for quantitating horizontal deviation, because accommodative convergence cannot be controlled. gastrointestinal (GI) workup A. 1% cardiac workup B. 7% metastatic workup C. 0% Explanation & Notes Discussion BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A child with bilateral optic nerve hypoplasia is found to have an absent septum pellucidum. What further workup is necessary?
explanation: The correct answer is an endocrine workup. De Morsier (septo-optic dysplasia) syndrome involves optic nerve hypoplasia, absent septum pellucidum, and pituitary dysfunction. The decreased pituitary function can be life-threatening, and any patient with concern for this syndrome should have rapid endocrine evaluation for the need of hormone replacement. question: A child has a visual acuity of 20/30 right eye and 20/20 left eye. Cover testing demonstrates a 4-diopter right esotropia. On Worth 4-dot testing, the child sees 3 lights at distance and 4 lights at near. What is this child demonstrating?
explanation: ARC is a condition wherein the fovea of the ﬁxating eye has acquired an anomalous common visual direction with a peripheral retinal element in the deviating eye. ARC is an adaptation that restores some degree of binocular cooperation despite manifest strabismus. Seeing 4 dots indicates that if there is a suppression scotoma, it must subtend a smaller visual angle than the test target. In this case, the right eye is suppressing the Worth 4-dot at distance, since the lights are being projected into the suppression scotoma. At near, the lights are outside the suppression scotoma and a fused response is noted. This is consistent with ARC. The child has ARC and monoﬁxation syndrome. The clinician must demonstrate the absence of bimacular fusion by documenting a macular scotoma in the nonﬁxating eye under binocular conditions, as well as the presence of peripheral binocular vision (peripheral fusion). A diplopic response or 5 lights would be given at near in normal retinal correspondence in this patient with a right esotropia. If a large suppression scotoma were present, only 3 lights would be seen at near. Paradoxical diplopia occurs when ARC persists following ocular realignment surgery and a previously misaligned eye is now straight. amblyopia.

question: What is the essential feature of monoﬁxation syndrome? anomalous retinal correspondence (ARC) C. 42 Correct Answer large suppression scotoma D.

options.C: presence of peripheral fusion with the absence of bifoveal fusion, due to a central scotoma

explanation: Monoﬁxation syndrome is a sensory state in strabismus where there is the presence of peripheral fusion with the absence of bifoveal fusion, due to a macular scotoma. Thus, amblyopia may be present in the deviated eye, along with a reduction of stereopsis. In a patient with monoﬁxation syndrome, the Worth 4-dot test can demonstrate both the presence of peripheral fusion and the absence of biﬁxation. The standard Worth 4-dot ﬂashlight projects onto a central retinal area of 1 degree or less when viewed at 3 m, well within the 1-4 degree scotoma characteristic of monoﬁxation syndrome, so patients with monoﬁxation syndrome report seeing 2 or 3 lights, depending on ﬁxation preference. As the Worth 4-dot ﬂashlight is brought closer to the patient, the dots project onto more peripheral retina outside the central monoﬁxation scotoma, and a fusion response (4 lights) is obtained. This usually occurs betwen 0.67 m and 1 m.

question: What features might be found when evaluating the brain scan and cerebrospinal ﬂuid of a child with idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri)?

options.A: normal-sized or small ventricles and abnormal cerebral ﬂuid composition
options.B: normal-sized or small ventricles and normal cerebrospinal ﬂuid composition
options.C: enlarged ventricles and abnormal cerebrospinal ﬂuid composition
options.D: enlarged ventricles and normal cerebrospinal ﬂuid composition

explanation: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), or pseudotumor cerebri, is characterized by an increase in intracranial pressure, normal-sized or small ventricles on neuroimaging, and normal cerebrospinal ﬂuid composition. IIH can occur in children of any age and has been associated with viral infections, drug use (tetracycline, corticosteroids, vitamin A, nalidixic acid, thyroid medications, growth hormone), and cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. Prepubescent children with IIH have a lower incidence of obesity compared with adult patients, and the male-to-female ratio is approximately equal. Postpubescent children with IIH have a clinical proﬁle similar to that of adults; they have a higher incidence of obesity, compared with younger patients, and a BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What abnormally developed ocular structure is the pathologic cause of primary congenital glaucoma?
explanation: The basic pathophysiologic defect in primary congenital glaucoma is decreased aqueous outﬂow due to abnormal development of neural crest–derived tissue of the anterior chamber angle. Although abnormalities of the Descemet membrane, iris, and optic nerve all occur in primary congenital glaucoma, they are secondary eﬀects from the increased intraocular pressure that occurs in this disease.

question: What is the most likely diagnosis in an infant with decreased vision and paradoxical pupillary responses?
explanation: Paradoxical pupils, a pupillary constriction in response to darkness, are most commonly associated with retinal dystrophies, although they can occur with optic neuropathies. Amblyopia is a unilateral, or less commonly, a bilateral reduction of best-corrected visual acuity that cannot be attributed directly to the eﬀect of any structural abnormality of the eye or visual pathways. Subtle aﬀerent pupillary defects occur rarely and only in severe cases of amblyopia, not a paradoxical pupillary response. Delayed visual maturation (DVM) is the condition wherein normal visual ﬁxation and tracking do not develop in an infant within the ﬁrst 3 months of life. Cortical or cerebral visual impairment (CVI) is a condition in which visual deﬁcits result from pathology posterior to the lateral geniculate nucleus. They usually have normal pupillary responses.

question: For a patient with dissociated vertical deviation (DVD), what motility anomaly accompanies the upward movement?

options.B: downward movement of the fellow eye on cover testing

explanation: Patients with dissociated strabismus can have accompanying extorsion and exodeviation (not esodeviation) of the elevating eye. Typically, there is no hypodeviation of the fellow eye on cover testing, due to an apparent violation of Hering's law of motor correspondence. DVD is usually seen in infantile strabismus. In this form of strabismus, any associated nystagmus is of the latent variety, which has a horizontal vector.

question: A 4-month-old girl is brought for evaluation because her eyes cross. Her cycloplegic refraction is +1.00 sphere in each eye. She has 40 prism diopters of constant esotropia in all directions of gaze. Using a toy for ﬁxation, the ophthalmologist notes bilateral abduction deﬁcits that resolve with patching each eye. No nystagmus is noted. What is the most appropriate long-term management for this patient to prevent the development of amblyopia?

options.D: patching each eye, alternating each day

explanation: This patient has infantile esotropia. Pertinent clinical features of infantile esotropia include a deviation characteristically greater than 30 prism diopters, overelevation in adduction, dissociated vertical deviation (DVD), and low hyperopia (1.00-2.00 diopters). Equal visual acuity is common, and an apparent abduction deﬁcit may result from cross-ﬁxation. The infant’s ability to abduct can be elicited by the doll’s head maneuver, spinning the infant to stimulate the vestibulo-ocular reﬂex, or by observation with either eye patched. These patients usually have full abduction unless there is secondary medial rectus muscle restriction. Hyperopia or astigmatism greater than +2.50 diopters suggests a refractive strabismus. Deviation in primary position of less than 30 prism diopters is uncommon in infantile esotropia. Deviations greater than 30 diopters are unlikely to resolve and will probably require surgical intervention; ocular alignment is rarely achieved without surgery in early-onset esotropia. The belief is that the eyes should be aligned by 2 years of age, preferably earlier, to optimize binocular cooperation. The Congenital Esotropia Observational Study showed that when patients present with constant esotropia of at least 40Δ after 10 weeks of age, the deviations are unlikely to resolve spontaneously. Smaller angles can be monitored, as they may improve spontaneously. Full cycloplegic refraction should be prescribed, but because there is minimal refractive error, this is unlikely to fully resolve the esotropia (ie, minimal accommodative component).

question: A 6-week-old boy presents with unilateral epiphora, blepharospasm, and photophobia. The cornea is enlarged but clear. The intraocular pressure (IOP) is 38 mm Hg. What is the preferred initial treatment?
explanation: The classic triad of congenital glaucoma is epiphora, photophobia, and blepharospasm. The initial treatment is surgical, with goniotomy or trabeculotomy preferred for the initial treatment. Primary trabeculectomy has a high failure rate and is contraindicated as primary treatment. Both Ahmed valve placement and cycloablation are reserved for secondary treatments. no adjustment; full correction should be given for both eyes A. 74% Correct Answer Explanation & Notes Discussion BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: In children with anisometropic amblyopia, what adjustments should be made to the glasses prescription to help with adaptation to the glasses?

options.A: no adjustment; full correction should be given for both eyes

explanation: In children with refractive amblyopia, full correction of both eyes is frequently well tolerated, and it may be suﬃcient to correct the amblyopia even without patching or atropine penalization. If undercorrection is needed, the amblyopic eye should be fully corrected and the other eye can be undercorrected. Slab-oﬀ prism can be used to reduce induced vertical prismatic eﬀects. Adjustments can be made to the lens base curve to minimize eﬀect on image size. topical.

question: A 32-year-old woman undergoes strabismus surgery with adjustable sutures. What type of anesthesia is the most appropriate for postoperative suture adjustment?
explanation: Topical anesthetic is most appropriate for adjustment of sutures postoperatively in adults. General anesthesia is necessary in children. Retrobulbar and sub-Tenon infusion are not indicated, because they can aﬀect ocular motility. autosomal dominant.

question: What is the most common inheritance pattern in inherited cases of congenital glaucoma?
explanation: Primary congenital glaucoma, also commonly called congenital or infantile glaucoma, usually occurs sporadically, but it can be inherited as an autosomal recessive trait. One gene, CYP1B1, on band 2p21, has been shown to cause primary congenital glaucoma. Juvenile-onset glaucoma and the anterior segment dysgenesis syndromes are inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. Leber hereditary optic neuropathy has mitochondrial inheritance.

question: What other ocular ﬁnding is most likely to be observed in the eye shown in the ﬁgure?
explanation: The ﬁgure shows a ﬁbrovascular stalk arising from the optic nerve and coursing through the vitreous towards the lens. This is an example of persistent fetal vasculature (PFV), which results from failure of regression of the primary vitreous and hyaloid artery. This condition is typically sporadic and unilateral. Its presentation varies from Bergmeister papillae or Mittendorf dot in the milder cases to a microphthalmic eye with retrolental plaque in more severe cases. Often elongated ciliary processes may be observed. The ﬁbrovascular stalk can exert traction onto the retina and lead to retinal detachment. Cataract may also form and may require early cataract extraction with membrane excision.

question: What is the most appropriate surgical management for a patient with unilateral superior oblique palsy where extorsion is the primary problem?
explanation: Treatment of superior oblique palsy typically involves strengthening the muscle with a tuck, weakening the antagonist inferior oblique muscle, or recessing the other elevator of the eye, the superior rectus muscle. However, all of these procedures are intended to correct the vertical misalignment. When the primary problem is extorsion, the Harada-Ito procedure is preferred. This operation involves displacement of the anterior portions of the superior oblique tendons to a location adjacent to the upper edge of the lateral rectus muscle, about 8.0 mm posterior to that muscle's insertion. Superior rectus recession and a Faden procedure may be part of surgical correction for a larger vertical deviation. Superior oblique tenotomy would be a treatment for superior oblique overaction.

question: A 71-year-old man presents with binocular diplopia on the morning following cataract surgery with retrobulbar anesthesia. What mechanism is most likely responsible for the diplopia?

options.B: brainstem toxicity related to subdural lidocaine injection

explanation: Injected local anesthesia can have a direct toxic eﬀect on muscle tissue. Hyaluronidase may be partially protective by allowing more rapid diﬀusion of the anesthetic agent. The inferior and superior recti are susceptible to direct injury with the needle in retrobulbar and peribulbar anesthesia, respectively. Inadvertent intravenous injection of local anesthetics can cause cardiac arrhythmia. Inadvertent intradural injection is associated with seizures, respiratory arrest, and brainstem anesthesia. Other complications of retrobulbar injection include retrobulbar hemorrhage and globe perforation. Other causes of binocular diplopia after cataract surgery could include disruption of fusion in predisposed patients. Surgically induced astigmatism could be associated with monocular diplopia. chondroitin sulfate.

question: What is the most likely mode of inheritance for the condition pictured?
explanation: Craniosynostosis is characterized by the premature closure of cranial suture lines. This can occur as an isolated abnormality or as a genetic syndrome with systemic abnormalities. The most common craniosynostosis syndrome is Crouzon syndrome, which is the only syndrome that does not have the hallmarks of syndactyly and brachydactyly. Typical ophthalmic features include exophthalmos, proptosis, globe luxation, corneal exposure, strabismus, and amblyopia. question: In a patient with achromatopsia, what characteristic ﬁndings are expected on the electroretinogram (ERG)?

options.A: severely abnormal scotopic response, and severely abnormal photopic response
options.B: severely abnormal scotopic response, but normal photopic response
options.C: normal scotopic response, but severely abnormal photopic response
options.D: normal scotopic response, and normal photopic response

explanation: Achromatopsia is a retinal disorder in which patients have no color vision, as well as poor central vision, nystagmus, and photophobia (rather than pain or discomfort, the photophobia represents a preference to avoid bright light); hemeralopia (inability to see clearly in bright light) also occurs in these patients. Achromatopsia is caused by deﬁcient cone function with normal rod functioning. ERG test results show normal scotopic response, but severely abnormal photopic response. Achromatopsia was initially thought to be a stationary disorder; however, recent studies have shown deterioration of visual acuity, macular appearance, and cone function on ERG. A poor scotopic and photopic response suggests a diﬀerent diagnosis, as does a normal ERG result.

question: A healthy 4-year-old boy with normal visual acuity in both eyes has a chin-up posture. What is the most likely cause of this boy's anomalous head position?
explanation: The most likely cause of this boy's abnormal chin-up position is V- pattern exotropia (ﬁgure). A-pattern or V-pattern strabismus occurs in up to one-fourth of all horizontal strabismus cases. Patients with V- pattern forms of strabismus have a horizontal deviation that is more convergent or less divergent in downgaze compared with upgaze. Patients with pattern strabismus and sensory fusion may adopt an anomalous head posture in an eﬀort to maintain a single image, for example, chin-up posture with V-pattern exotropia or chin-down posture with A-pattern exotropia. The etiology of pattern strabismus is unknown except in cases of extraocular muscle palsies. Despite this, multiple theories suggest primary or secondary muscle dysfunction involving the oblique muscles, horizontal rectus muscles, or vertical rectus muscles. In A-pattern exotropia, a chin-up position would place the eyes in a position of increased exodeviation. question: Lisch nodules in neuroﬁbromatosis type 1 are composed of what type of abnormal cellular growth?
explanation: Ocular ﬁndings in neuroﬁbromatosis type 1 (NF1) include Lisch nodules (ﬁgure), prominent corneal nerves, and choroidal hamartomas. Lisch nodules are ﬂat or dome-shaped iris nodules, usually less than 1 mm and tan to dark brown in color. They are hamartomas (tissue normally found at the site, but in increased amounts). Schwann cells, ﬁbroblast- like cells, and mast cells have been identiﬁed in biopsies of Lisch nodules, supporting neural crest origin. Lisch nodules are present in 10% of children with NF1 at 1 year of age, but in nearly 100% by age 10. The presence of 2 or more Lisch nodules is one of the criteria for the diagnosis of NF1 (6 or more cafe-au-lait spots; 2 or more neuroﬁbromas; intertriginous freckling; optic nerve glioma; Lisch nodules; distinctive osseous lesions; ﬁrst-degree relative with NF1). The NF1 gene is located at chromosome 17 q11.20, and its product, neuroﬁbromin, is a tumor suppressant. The loss of neuroﬁbromin leads to cell and tumor growth. Lisch nodules diﬀer from iris mammillations, which are smaller, diﬀuse nodules on the iris surface, but which are the same color as the iris. f653- 4bd1- b4cf- c03f459fcd36) .

question: Relative to the globe, what is the most common location of a congenital orbital dermoid cyst?
explanation: Dermoid cysts are thought to arise from entrapped epithelial nests during embryogenesis. They can take on a dumbbell shape as they protrude through the frontozygomatic or frontomaxillary sutures. The cysts are encapsulated and lined by keratinized stratiﬁed squamous epithelium with associated adnexal structures. Because of the location of these sutures, the most common location relative to the globe is the superotemporal quadrant of the orbit.

question: What approach is most eﬀective in ensuring that a patient's parents or caregivers adhere to an amblyopia treatment plan?

options.C: occlusion therapy by covering the amblyopic eye
options.D: counseling regarding treatment and side eﬀects

explanation: Counseling regarding treatment and side eﬀects is an important part of amblyopia treatment, because the outcome often depends on patient compliance. Parents and caregivers are more likely to adhere to treatment recommendations if they understand the diagnosis and rationale for treatment. In older children, it is important to obtain their commitment to the treatment program. In compliant patients, improvement is frequent but cannot be guaranteed. Future work opportunities also cannot be determined. Occlusion therapy is performed by covering the patient's better-seeing eye, not the amblyopic eye.

question: An ophthalmologist is asked by the neonatal department to evaluate a premature infant for a possible embryogenetic defect. If the child has bilateral anophthalmia, at what stage did embryogenesis fail?

options.A: There were abnormalities in branchial cleft formation.
options.B: The embryonic ﬁssure did not close.
options.C: The choroidal ﬁssure did not close.
options.D: The optic vesicle did not grow out from the cerebral vesicle.

explanation: The ﬁrst step in ocular embryogenesis is the formation of the optic vesicle, which evaginates from the forebrain toward surface ectoderm. If this step fails, anophthalmia (also termed anophthalmos) results. The remaining choices describe progressive developmental steps in ocular formation. Failure of any particular step results in speciﬁc developmental abnormalities that are seen clinically. Failure of embryonic ﬁssure closure results in coloboma formation of the optic nerve head. Branchial cleft abnormalities typically present as surface deformities deﬁned by the Tessier system, with cleft palate and lip being the most common examples on the face. Multiple clefting patterns may occur in BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A 3-year-old child has a history of primary infantile glaucoma. The child's condition remains poorly controlled despite maximal medical therapy and previous goniotomy on 2 separate occasions. What is the most appropriate next step in treatment?
explanation: Surgical intervention is the treatment of choice for primary congenital glaucoma presenting in infancy and early childhood. Angle surgery (ie, goniotomy or trabeculotomy) is the preferred initial surgical intervention. Usually, a second angle surgery is attempted before proceeding to alternative surgical interventions. If this fails, then the best next procedure is the placement of a glaucoma drainage device implant with a Molteno, Baerveldt, or Ahmed device.

question: For acquired esotropia, the maximal angle of strabismus and fusional potential can be assessed by what test?
explanation: In prism adaptation, the patient with acquired esotropia is ﬁtted with prisms to induce orthophoria. The patient is reexamined every 1 to 2 weeks, and the prism correction is increased until a stable amount of prism to achieve orthophoria is found. More prism correction is often needed at each visit. The double Maddox rod test is dissociative and cannot be used to determine fusional potential. Likewise, a 30-minute patch test is a dissociative test, so it cannot determine fusional potential. The Lancaster red-green test does not determine the maximal angle of strabismus.

question: In congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction, when is silicone intubation used?

options.A: for procedures on babies aged 1-6 months with epiphora
options.B: when a Jones tube is placed along with simple probing or balloon dilation
options.D: when 1 or more simple probing or balloon dilations have failed

explanation: Intubation of the nasolacrimal system is usually recommended when one or more initial probings have failed. Surgical intervention is not recommended in infants without complications who are younger than 12 months, since the nasolacrimal duct obstruction may resolve spontaneously. Older children and adults have a diﬀerent etiology for epiphora, which must be addressed based on the ﬁndings. If a Jones tube is placed, silicone intubation is unnecessary. Probing should be done for dacryocystoceles to prevent complications related to infection.

question: An adult with Parkinson disease has symptoms of asthenopia, blurred near vision, and problems reading. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Convergence insuﬃciency is a convergence weakness exotropia that presents with no or minimal deviation at distance but an exotropia at near, with poor fusional convergence amplitudes and a remote near point of convergence. Treatment can include orthoptic exercises, prisms, or in some cases surgery, consisting of medial rectus resections.

question: Aside from conjunctivitis, what condition is typically associated with Chlamydia trachomatis acquired by a neonate during childbirth?
explanation: Chlamydia trachomatis can be transferred during sexual contact with others or during childbirth. In adults, it usually aﬀects the eyes in the form of inclusion conjunctivitis or as trachoma. In newborns, it can manifest as ophthalmia neonatorum and as pneumonia. It is important to be aware of the systemic infectious potential when treating a newborn with chlamydia conjunctivitis, which is why treatment for neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis consists of oral erythromycin 50 mg/kg per day, divided into 12.5 mg/kg doses, 4 times daily for 14 days. Interstitial keratitis can be seen with syphilis. Koplik spots are whitish lesions, found on the inside of the mouth, that are highly characteristic of the early phase of measles (rubeola). Hearing loss often accompanies cytomegalovirus (CMV) congenital infections.

question: An 11-month-old girl presents for evaluation and is found to have epiblepharon. The child is playful and asymptomatic, and there is no evidence of corneal involvement. What would be the best initial management for her condition?

question: A 4-year-old patient has new esotropia of a similar angle at distance and near. His refractive error is +4.00 D. When he wears glasses with the full correction, his vision is good in both eyes and his eyes are straight. What type of esotropia is this?
explanation: Refractive accommodative esotropia occurs in the setting of uncorrected hyperopia with accommodative convergence with insuﬃcient fusional divergence, leading to an esotropia. The angle is approximately the same at distance and near ﬁxation and is generally between 20 and 30 prism diopters. The average amount of hyperopia in refractive accommodative esotropia is +4.00 D. In high AC/A ratio accommodative esotropia, patients have an excessive convergence response for the amount of accommodation required to focus. The deviation is only present at near or is much larger at near. In divergence insuﬃciency, the deviation is greater at distance than at near. question: What is the most likely ocular ﬁnding in a neonate with congenital rubella syndrome (CRS)?
explanation: A unilateral or bilateral pigmentary retinopathy is the most common ocular manifestation of CRS (25%–50%), followed by cataract (15%) and glaucoma (10%). The pigmentary disturbance, often described as “salt-and-pepper” fundus, shows considerable variation, ranging from ﬁnely stippled, bone spicule–like, small, black, irregular masses to gross pigmentary irregularities with coarse, blotchy mottling. It can be stationary or progressive. Despite loss of the foveal light reﬂex and prominent pigmentary changes, neither vision nor electroretinogram results are typically aﬀected. Congenital (nuclear) cataracts and microphthalmia are the most frequent causes of poor visual acuity and, rarely, choroidal neovascularization (CNV). Unless otherwise compromised by glaucoma, the optic nerve and the retinal vessels are typically normal in appearance.

question: What is the most appropriate method of visual acuity testing in a typical 3- to 4-year-old child?
explanation: Visual acuity testing is dependent upon age and whether the child knows the letters of the alphabet. The Snellen acuity test is the gold standard, but in children ages 2 to 5, matching tests such as the HOTV and LEA symbols might be cognitively easier. Teller acuity testing is typically reserved for preverbal infants, or children with cognitive and verbal delays. Allen ﬁgures are not well standardized and may be culturally biased.

question: A patient is found to have A- pattern exotropia with compensatory head posture. What is the most likely head posture?
explanation: In an A-pattern exotropia, the misalignment is more exotropic in downgaze and less exotropic in upgaze. Therefore, the patient may adopt a chin-down position to decrease or eliminate the misalignment. A chin-up position would worsen the alignment. A-pattern strabismus does not typically have lateral incomitance, so left and right face turns will not improve or worsen the alignment.

question: An infant presents with a hyperacute unilateral conjunctivitis, as shown in the image. What treatment is recommended?
explanation: The image shows ophthalmia neonatorum with purulent discharge caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Ophthalmia neonatorum from Neisseria gonorrhoeae typically presents in the ﬁrst 3-4 days of life. Cultures should be obtained, and treatment includes systemic ceftriaxone and topical irrigation with saline. Neisseria gonorrhoeae may be associated with meningitis and sepsis and Chlamydia may be associated with pneumonia. Topical antibiotics will not treat systemic disease, but they can be used as an adjunct in cases with corneal involvement. Silver nitrate is prophylaxis, not treatment.

question: What constitutes the classic clinical triad of primary congenital glaucoma?

options.B: photophobia, corneal edema, and corneal enlargement
options.C: corneal edema, Haab striae, and buphthalmos

explanation: Epiphora, photophobia, and blepharospasm constitute the classical clinical triad of primary congenital glaucoma. Other signs include clouding and enlargement of the cornea (ﬁrst ﬁgure). Photophobia, epiphora, and blepharospasm result from the glare and epithelial abnormalities associated with corneal edema and opaciﬁcation. Corneal edema results from elevated IOP and may be gradual or sudden in onset. Corneal edema is often the presenting sign in infants younger than 3 months. Microcystic edema initially involves the corneal epithelium but later extends to the stroma, often accompanied by one or more curvilinear breaks in Descemet membrane (Haab striae, second ﬁgure). Although the corneal edema may resolve with IOP reduction, a scar will remain permanently at the site of the Haab striae. A number of other conditions may also cause corneal edema or Descemet tears (such as birth trauma). Corneal enlargement occurs with gradual stretching of the cornea as a result of elevated IOP. A corneal diameter of greater than 11.5 mm is suggestive of glaucoma in a newborn, while a diameter greater than 12.5 mm suggests glaucoma at the age of 1 year. Glaucoma should be suspected in any child with a corneal diameter greater than 13.0 mm. Blepharophimosis is not a clinical feature of primary congenital glaucoma. ddd8- 4a80- aa92- cf6df0c063fb)  bb33- 55d6600bfb58) .

question: A 12-month-old child is brought to the oﬃce with recurrent unilateral pink eye despite numerous courses of antibiotics, as well as lacrimal sac massage. What would be the preferred treatment?

options.B: insertion of lacrimal stent in the oﬃce
options.C: probing and irrigation of the nasolacrimal system under general anesthesia
options.D: continued massage of the lacrimal sac twice a day

explanation: Nasolacrimal duct obstruction is present in 5%-20% of newborns. It is most commonly caused by a persistent membrane at the valve of Hasner. It can resolve spontaneously in the ﬁrst 9 to 12 months of life. Early treatment consists of lacrimal sac massage and antibiotic usage.

question: What type of nystagmus is commonly associated with esotropia?
explanation: Fusion maldevelopment nystagmus syndrome is a marker of fusion maldevelopment such as in infantile esotropia. When 1 eye is occluded, a conjugate jerk nystagmus occurs, with fast phase toward the ﬁxating eye. This is the only form of nystagmus that changes direction with a change in ﬁxation.

question: What is the most common type of leukemia in children?
explanation: Acute leukemias tend to have the most severe manifestations, with a rapid onset and course. Leukemia in childhood is acute in 95% of cases and is more commonly lymphocytic than myelocytic. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is the most common malignant disease of childhood. It is responsible for 30% of all cancer cases. In the US, there are 4000 new cases per year. The most common ocular BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: In a patient with infantile nystagmus, what symptom does a Kestenbaum or an Anderson procedure primarily ameliorate?
explanation: A compensatory head-turn into the null point occurs frequently in patients with infantile nystagmus syndrome. A Kestenbaum procedure (a recession-resection procedure in both eyes) or an Anderson procedure (a medial rectus recession in 1 eye and lateral rectus recession in the other), via recession-resection, corrects this anomalous head position by shifting the null point closer to the primary position.

question: For 3 months, an 8-year-old child has had irritation and discharge in her left eye (ﬁgure). What virus is associated with this condition?
explanation: The ﬁgure depicts a molluscum contagiosum lesion. Molluscum contagiosum is a viral infection of the skin caused by a DNA poxvirus and generally occurs in children and immunocompromised patients. It is spread through direct contact or shared items such as clothing or towels. When it aﬀects the periocular skin, it may result in follicular conjunctivitis. Primary herpes simplex 1 virus can manifest as a grouped vesicular eruption around the periocular skin. Parvovirus B19 causes a childhood rash called ﬁfth disease, which is commonly called slapped cheek syndrome. Human papillomavirus 6 and 11 have been associated with conjunctival papillomas and verruca vulgaris (common wart).

question: A 3-year-old boy presents with intermittent esotropia and mild amblyopia of the right eye. On examination, there is an esodeviation of 30 prism diopters. Cycloplegic refraction is +4.50 OU. What is the most appropriate initial management?
explanation: This child presents with an esotropic deviation and is at an age typical of a patient with accommodative esotropia. The refraction of signiﬁcant hyperopia suggests that this is indeed accommodative esotropia, and glasses for the hyperopic correction should be prescribed. Surgery or botulinum toxin injection should not be performed unless there is residual esotropia after all the hyperopia is corrected for with glasses. Atropine penalization is used to treat amblyopia, but the ﬁrst step is full time spectacle correction.

question: What is the most common and serious ocular complication in the child pictured in the ﬁgure?
explanation: Port-wine stain on the eyelid, choroidal hemangioma, retinal vascular tortuosity, and glaucoma are all found in encephalofacial angiomatosis (also called Sturge-Weber syndrome). However, glaucoma is the most serious ocular complication and can be quite diﬃcult to control. Note the buphthalmos in the ﬁgure shown, on the side of the port-wine stain, because glaucoma can be present at birth. However, it can occur later in childhood as well. It has been reported to occur in up to approximately 70% of encephalofacial angiomatosis patients. Causes of elevated IOP include elevated episcleral venous pressure, hyperemia of the ciliary body with hypersecretion of aqueous, and developmental anomaly of the anterior chamber angle. Encephalofacial angiomatosis consists of a facial cutaneous angioma (port-wine stain), which is composed of well-formed capillaries in the dermis and usually involves the forehead and upper eyelid. The lesion can extend to the lower eyelid and maxillary and mandibular regions and does not always conform to the distribution of the trigeminal divisions. The eye ipsilateral to the port-wine stain may have tortuous vessels and arteriovenous communications in the retina and choroidal angiomatosis (ketchup fundus). Choroidal hemangiomas are asymptomatic in childhood; however, in adolescence or adulthood, the choroid sometimes becomes markedly thickened. Degeneration or detachment of the overlying retina with severe vision loss may occur; however, this is less common than glaucoma. The likelihood of glaucoma is increased if there is involvement of the upper eyelid skin, choroidal hemangioma, iris heterochromia, and episcleral hemangioma. Other serious nonocular complications include cerebral calciﬁcations and seizures, and leptomeningeal vascular malformations ipsilateral to the skin lesion.

question: What ocular condition are curvilinear tears in Descemet membrane most often seen in?
explanation: Tears in Descemet membrane (Haab striae) are seen because of a rapid stretching of the cornea in primary congenital glaucoma. They are not seen in congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy (CHED) or Peters anomaly. Trauma from amniocentesis can result in a penetrating injury of the cornea. Tears in Descemet membrane can also be seen in a forceps injury sustained during delivery, but these are usually linear, not curvilinear.

question: What syndrome is most commonly associated with the congenital eyelid abnormality shown below?
explanation: Eyelid colobomas are commonly associated with Goldenhar syndrome. They usually involve the upper eyelid and can range from a small notch to the absence of the entire length of the eyelid, which can sometimes be fused to the globe. Eyelid colobomas have also been associated with amniotic band syndrome. Waardenburg syndrome type 1 is associated with dystopia canthorum, in which there is lateral displacement of both the lateral canthi and lacrimal puncta. In this condition an imaginary line connecting upper and lower puncta crosses the cornea. Apert syndrome causes eyelid malposition secondary to forehead and superior retrusion and other craniofacial abnormalities. Stickler syndrome is associated with midface ﬂattening.

question: What is the etiology of primary congenital glaucoma in most patients?
explanation: Primary congenital glaucoma usually occurs sporadically, but it can rarely be inherited as an autosomal recessive trait. Speciﬁc genetic mutations have been identiﬁed in some patients.

question: A 10-year-old child is evaluated for a right hypertropia noted after closed head trauma. Upon covering the left eye, the uncovered right eye depresses, while the covered left eye elevates. What is the most likely cause of this child's strabismus?
explanation: When evaluating a vertical deviation, cover testing helps assess the relationship between the elevators and depressors of the 2 eyes. In this case, the covered left eye violates Hering's law by elevating instead of depressing. This anomalous movement is consistent with dissociated vertical deviation, found in individuals with infantile strabismus. If the child had a paralytic strabismus (such as a right 4th nerve palsy) or a restrictive strabismus (such as one secondary to a posterior orbital ﬂoor fracture), the left eye would adopt a hypotropic position. Poor vision after trauma can cause a sensory strabismus, but is typically horizontal, and on cover testing the poor-seeing eye may not be able to reestablish ﬁxation.

question: A child has asthma, eczema, chronic tearing, and red eyes. Examination shows papillae of the palpebral conjunctiva and punctate corneal erosions. The patient is already using a combination topical H-1 blocker and mast cell stabilizer, in addition to an oral antihistamine. Given the corneal involvement indicating severe disease, what topical medication should be used?
explanation: Atopic keratoconjunctivitis is a chronic ocular surface allergy-related inﬂammatory disorder. It is characterized by a history of asthma and eczema in association with ocular ﬁndings of papillae and chronic tearing. More severe ﬁndings include punctate corneal erosions, epithelial defects, and neovascularization. Topical medications include mast-cell stabilizers, H -receptor antagonists, antihistamines, vasoconstrictors, corticosteroids, or combinations of these drugs. 1 BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What condition is associated with an abnormally high number of crossed ﬁbers in the optic chiasm?
explanation: Ocular albinism is associated with iris transillumination, foveal aplasia or hypoplasia, and decreased retinal pigmentation. Both human and animal studies have shown an abnormally high number of crossed ﬁbers in the optic chiasm, which precludes stereopsis and is associated with strabismus. Optic nerve hypoplasia and morning glory disc are not BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: For pediatric patients with presumed retinoblastoma, why are magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and ultrasonography the preferred imaging modalities, rather than computed tomography (CT) scan?

options.A: MRI and ultrasonography are better at detecting calcium in the tumor.
options.B: CT scan subjects the child to radiation.
options.C: MRI and ultrasonography are easier to obtain in a child.
options.D: MRI and ultrasonography are better at showing bony abnormalities in the orbit.

explanation: Unlike MRI and ultrasonography, a CT scan subjects patients to radiation. Children with heritable retinoblastoma are at high risk for secondary radiation-induced tumors, so any additional radiation should be avoided if possible.

question: To test for a horizontal deviation using the Maddox rod, what direction should the cylinders be oriented in front of the right eye?
explanation: In the Maddox rod test, a series of parallel cylinders convert a single point source of light into a line image perpendicular to the cylinders. To test for horizontal deviations, the Maddox rod cylinders are placed horizontally in front of the right eye (180°). The patient, ﬁxating on a point source of light, sees a vertical line with the right eye and the BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: An 18-month-old child demonstrates an asymmetric, high-frequency, small amplitude ( shimmering ) nystagmus, associated with head nodding. Neuroimaging is normal. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation: Spasmus nutans is an idiopathic, asymmetric, high-frequency, small amplitude ("shimmering") nystagmus, associated with head nodding. It manifests during the ﬁrst 2 years of life. The natural history is for the BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What type of urinalysis is the most appropriate for establishing the diagnosis of neuroblastoma?
explanation: Neuroblastoma is one of the more common childhood tumors that frequently have orbital manifestations. The primary tumor is typically in the adrenal glands or sympathetic ganglion chain. Urine BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What ancillary test best diagnoses Leber congenital amaurosis?
explanation: Leber congenital amaurosis is a group of hereditary retinal dystrophies that aﬀect both the rod and cone photoreceptors. It is characterized by severe vision loss in infancy, nystagmus, and poorly reactive pupils. An electroretinogram is typically used to make the diagnosis, showing extinguished waveforms. A-scan ultrasonography, ﬂuorescein angiography, and optical coherence tomography would not be helpful in making the diagnosis.

question: Constant tearing with copious mucus discharge in the infant shown suggests what condition?
explanation: Constant tearing with copious mucus discharge suggests nasolacrimal duct obstruction. Constant tearing with minimal mucopurulence suggests punctal or canalicular agenesis. Intermittent tearing with mucus discharge suggests intermittent obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct, most likely due to swollen inferior turbinate mucosa associated with upper respiratory tract infection or allergy. Congenital glaucoma is not associated with mucus discharge.

question: What is the most common form of childhood leukemia?
explanation: The most common type of leukemia in children is acute lymphoblastic leukemia (75%-80%). Acute myelogenous leukemia (20%-25%) and chronic myelogenous leukemia (<5%) are much less common. The most common ocular manifestation of leukemia is leukemic retinopathy, but all ocular structures can be aﬀected, and ocular involvement is highly correlated with central nervous system involvement.

question: Galactosemia, if left untreated, will result in what ocular condition?
explanation: Galactosemia leads to the development of cataracts, typically with an "oil droplet" appearance. The cataracts may resolve with dietary restriction before a child is 4 months old. Because a lack of treatment leads to cataracts and intellectual deﬁciency, the ophthalmologist can play an important role in preventing these complications by helping to make the correct diagnosis. Retinal degeneration, corneal clouding, and a central macular cherry red spot are results of other inborn errors of metabolism.

question: A 4-year-old boy presents with the fundus ﬁndings shown in the ﬁgures and cataracts in both eyes. What congenital infection did he most likely have?
explanation: Congenital rubella syndrome is caused by rubella virus that is transmitted transplacentally to a fetus. Eye ﬁndings include a variable pigmentary retinopathy, ranging from a salt-and-pepper appearance to a pseudoretinitis pigmentosa. In this case, the patient has macular pigmentary changes, as well as peripheral pigmentary changes. Other BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What is the most signiﬁcant risk factor for developing retinopathy of prematurity (ROP)?
explanation: The 2 strongest risk factors for ROP are gestational age and birth weight. Although race and lung disease are also risk factors, they are not as signiﬁcant as gestational age and birth weight. There is no diﬀerence in the risk of ROP between the sexes.

question: An infant has a capillary hemangioma involving the right eyelid, as shown. This child is at greatest risk of developing what type of amblyopia?
explanation: Ptosis can cause deprivational or anisometropic amblyopia. The eyelid can cover the visual axis or induce astigmatism in the aﬀected eye, causing an anisometropic amblyopia. In this case, occlusion of the visual axis presents the greatest risk for visual deprivation amblyopia. The child may develop a chin-up head position in order to use the eye with ptosis. Strabismic amblyopia would result from eye misalignment. Ametropic amblyopia would occur due to high refractive error. Meridional amblyopia refers to a speciﬁc variety of isoametropic amblyopia in which bilateral high astigmatic errors decrease resolving ability due to chronically blurred meridians.

question: A child with uncorrected infantile esotropia and manifest latent nystagmus has a face turn to the left. This head posture is most likely related to what?
explanation: Latent nystagmus occurs in children who have decreased fusion from early onset strabismus. When one eye is occluded, a jerk nystagmus develops in both eyes with the fast phase directed toward the uncovered eye. The null point is with the ﬁxating eye in adduction. Latent nystagmus becomes manifest when both eyes are open but only 1 eye is being used for vision. Thus, in a child with manifest latent nystagmus, on ﬁxation with the left eye, the null zone would be on adduction leading to a face turn to the left.

question: What are the cardinal positions of gaze?

options.A: up and right, up and left, down and right, down and left, right head tilt, left head tilt
options.B: up and right, up and left, right, left, down and right, down and left
options.C: ﬁxating straight ahead at distance and near
options.D: straight up, straight down, right, left

explanation: The positions of gaze are: Primary position is the position of the eyes when they are ﬁxating straight ahead. Secondary diagnostic positions are straight up, straight down, right gaze, and left gaze. Tertiary diagnostic positions are the 4 oblique positions of gaze: up and right, up and left, down and right, down and left, as well as the right and left head-tilt positions. Cardinal positions, which correspond to the primary ﬁelds of action of the extraocular muscles (EOMs), are up and right, up and left, right, left, down and right, down and left. 0cbe- 4b51- 9a05- 8c5cbd29d244&t=636755759923200000)

question: A 68-year-old woman has a large esodeviation secondary to a complete sixth nerve palsy OD that has not resolved for 9 months. She cannot abduct past midline. What treatment is indicated?

options.A: botulinum toxin injection to the ipsilateral medial rectus muscle
options.C: large resection of the involved lateral rectus muscle with recession of the ipsilateral medial rectus muscle

explanation: Surgery for the treatment of 6th nerve palsy is indicated when spontaneous resolution does not occur after 6 months or more of follow-up. In patients with some lateral rectus muscle function, a large recession of the antagonist medial rectus muscle, combined with resection of the lateral rectus muscle, is appropriate. However, in cases of total paralysis like this one, a vertical muscle transposition procedure is usually required. Botulinum toxin injection into the ipsilateral medial rectus muscle can be used initially to balance the paretic lateral rectus muscle while waiting for potential spontaneous improvement in 6th nerve function. Orthoptic exercises would not be useful.
